description: Leather body armor was used by many ancient cultures as a relatively lightweight and accessible form of protection, particularly for soldiers who could not afford extensive metal armor. Thick hides could be hardened, layered, stitched, or reinforced with metal fittings to create cuirasses, corselets, and protective panels that offered useful defense against cuts, glancing blows, and some missile impacts while remaining more flexible than bronze or iron armor. Leather defenses were especially practical for cavalry, skirmishers, and poorer infantry, though their archaeological survival is limited because organic materials decay far more readily than metal.
